chunks: By Allah, if you weep with the weeping of a she-camel for her young, call out with the cooing of pigeons, and cry out with the crying of devoted monks, and depart to Allah from your wealth and children seeking nearness to Him in the elevation of a rank with Him or the forgiveness of a sin recorded by His books and preserved by His angels, it would be little of what I hope for you from His reward and fear for you from His punishment.

key_terms.الزُّهَّادِ: the ascetics / those who practice zuhd (detachment from the world)
key_terms.حَنِينَ الْوُلَّهِ الْعِجَالِ: the weeping of a she-camel for her young calf
key_terms.مُتَبَتِّلِي الرُّهْبَانِ: devoted monks / those who have taken religious vows

ai.seo_question: What metaphors does Imam Ali use to describe the intensity of devotion required for spiritual reward?
ai.summary: Imam Ali employs hyperbolic imagery of animal cries and monastic seclusion to argue that even the most intense worldly detachment is insufficient compared to the magnitude of divine reward he anticipates for his audience. This reflects the Shia emphasis on *ittiba'* (following the Imams) as the surest path to *qurbah* (nearness to God), contrasting superficial asceticism with the sincere, comprehensive devotion required to erase recorded sins. The passage underscores the balance between hope in God's mercy and fear of His justice, a core theme in Shia spiritual psychology.

en.sayed-ali-raza: By Allāh, if you cry like the she-camel that has lost its young one, call out like the cooing of pigeons, make noise like devoted recluses and turn to Allāh leaving your wealth and children as a means to secure His nearness and high position with Him or the forgiveness of sins which have been covered by His books and recorded by His angels it would be less than His reward that I expect for you or His retribution that I fear about you.
